extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of history, literary criticism, and moral philosophy interested in the nature of heroes and heroic leadership
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing historical figures (heroes) by their moral character, relation to reality, practical effectiveness, sincerity, and lasting impact as discussed in a literary-critical essay. Focus is on criteria Carlyle uses to judge heroes like Cromwell and Napoleon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity / Inner conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero possesses genuine inward belief or conviction (religious or moral) that animates action rather than mere performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle contrasts Cromwell's deep believing nature—'walking with God'—with Napoleon's lesser or more superficial sincerity. Sincerity is presented as fundamental: it gives purpose and seriousness to a man's deeds and survives awkward or broken utterance; lack of it leads to charlatanry and eventual ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action over polished utterance (authentic but inarticulate speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true hero may be inarticulate or speak in broken, chaotic phrases, because his primary reality is action rather than rhetorical polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cromwell's 'shapeless, involved chaotic' speeches are read as signs of a man who 'acts' the great inorganic thought rather than composes it; Carlyle advises to 'try to believe that he means something' and to search lovingly for the real speech imprisoned in rude utterances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with Reality and Facts (avoidance of Semblance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroes are judged by whether they return mankind to Reality and Fact rather than dwelling in semblance, sham, or theatrical contrivance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The French Revolution is praised as a return to reality; Napoleon's later apostasy into 'Semblances' (ceremonies, dynastic theatricality) is criticized as betrayal of the true work. Carlyle repeatedly contrasts grounding in fact with building on 'cloud' or tinsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to translate events into institutions / organize victory
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero should help convert victories and events into stable, rational, organized institutions or laws that endure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cromwell reproached Parliament to 'assemble together, and say in what manner all this could be organized,' implying that heroism includes the power to shape durable political or social order from revolutionary fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total commitment / refusal to resign
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine hero is one who, once embarked on his mission, cannot simply give it up — his path is irreversible and demands continuous bearing of burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle notes Cromwell 'could not get resigned' and 'let him once resign... Charles Stuart and the Cavaliers waited to kill him,' using this to argue that certain leaders are compelled to persist by circumstances and conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness / moral honesty (no liberty to tell lies)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero must maintain honesty; telling lies is morally wrong and strategically self-defeating because it destroys future credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle asserts 'A man in no case has liberty to tell lies' and warns that lies, once discovered, make it impossible to be believed even when telling truth; he criticizes Napoleon's frequent false bulletins as a grave fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical instinct / focus on the practical heart of matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroes show an instinct for what is practical and real, perceiving and acting on the core, effective element in a situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Napoleon's knack for seeing the practical—cutting a tassel to reveal tinsel—his insistence on 'there is no result in it' when quarrelling is pointless; Carlyle values this practical orientation as part of greatness when it is grounded in reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith in a larger movement or cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero perceives and embraces a broad, enduring social or moral Fact (e.g., democracy, Providence) and aligns personal action with that movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Napoleon's early insight that the French Revolution was an 'unsuppressible Fact' and Cromwell's belief in 'births of Providence' are both cited as examples where faith in a larger reality empowers heroic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hating anarchy while supporting popular movement (balancing order and revolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero supports the energies of popular change but equally detests and resists anarchic disorder; he seeks to 'tame' or organize revolution rather than let it consume itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle credits Napoleon with both a faith in democratic forces and a 'heart-hatred for anarchy,' seeing the hero's role as imposing authority to make revolution 'organic' and livable among formed institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of the charlatan-element and theatrical self-deception
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness is undermined when a leader succumbs to theatricality, self-deception, or the impulse to appear rather than be; the 'charlatan-element' makes achievements transient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle diagnoses Napoleon's fall as entering into 'strong delusion' and building on 'tinsel'—mixing ambition, ceremonial, and false symbols—thus turning living reality into mere semblance and hastening ruin. He warns that this element exists in all men and is fatal if developed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice of actions and moral consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero's ultimate measure is the justice of his deeds; actions that are unjust produce long-term recoil and moral compound-interest against the actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle cites acts like the execution of Palm as 'palpable tyrannous murderous injustice' that burn deep into hearts and provoke eventual uprising; in the long run 'what he did will amount to what he did justly.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability / organic vs ephemeral impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge heroes by whether their work becomes organic and lasting in society, or whether it is a 'flash'—a brilliant but transitory spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Napoleon's achievements are likened to a gunpowder flash—'a blazing-up' that 'goes out'—whereas genuine heroic work should yield enduring, formed results; the 'charlatan' tendency produces only smoke and waste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of symbols and inaugurations
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero's symbols, rituals, and inaugurations should be authentic and rooted in the real faith/authority of the movement, not theatrical contrivances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle praises Cromwell's Inauguration 'by the Sword and Bible' as genuinely true emblems, whereas Napoleon's coronations and concordats are condemned as theatrical paper-mantles that mask self-deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public recognition and moral fit (whether people see the hero as 'such')
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of heroic status is the perception by the public and soldiers that the person is the fitting embodiment of a movement or need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle notes 'All men saw that he _was_ such' about Napoleon's rise—public conviction that a man is the right instrument for his age is treated as evidence of his heroic office (though not sufficient by itself).

rubrics_metrics.name: Being an 'implement' for a larger truth (leaving unfinished potential)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero may serve as an 'implement' or rough draft (ébauche) for a larger historical truth or future fulfillment; greatness can be an initial, incomplete articulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle calls Napoleon a 'great ébauche, a rude-draught never completed'—a man who articulated some truths (e.g., 'La carriere ouverte aux talens') but left them inarticulate for future realization; this assesses a hero by durable seeds left behind even if imperfectly realized.
